note: NO ABSOLUTE HUMAN ACCURACY IS IMPORTED HERE, AND THAT IS A METHODOLOGICAL POSITION RATHER THAN A GAP. Pilly, P. K. & Seitz, A. R. (2009), 'What a difference a parameter makes: A psychophysical comparison of random dot motion algorithms', Vision Research 49(13):1599-1612 (PMID 19336240), shows that direction-discrimination performance in random-dot displays depends heavily on implementation details - the noise algorithm (Brownian vs white-noise vs limited-lifetime), dot density, speed, aperture, and duration - and concludes that this 'makes it difficult to make cross-study comparisons'. Importing a percent-correct value from any study whose algorithm differs from this port's would be exactly the cross-study comparison that paper warns against. This port uses a custom canvas implementation with 200 dots and a 2,000 ms stimulus at coherences 0.05/0.10/0.20/0.40/0.80; no published human study matches that configuration. WHAT IS SOURCED IS THE SHAPE, AND THAT IS WHAT L3 TESTS. Roitman, J. D. & Shadlen, M. N. (2002), J. Neurosci. 22(21):9475-9490 establishes the monotonic psychometric and chronometric functions across coherence - accuracy rising and reaction time falling as coherence increases. Their raw data and code are public (shadlenlab.columbia.edu/resources/RoitmanDataCode.html), so that claim is independently checkable. It is a TWO-MACAQUE study with LIP recordings and constrains ordering across coherence, never a human absolute level. The L3 signatures test exactly the sourced part: that accuracy is above chance and ordered across coherence. L2 does not read the ordering, only the levels, so overall_accuracy 0.79 and the per-coherence values 0.60/0.85/0.97 are AUTHOR ESTIMATES anchored to that shape. A previous attribution of the human levels to 'Pinet et al. (2024)' was WITHDRAWN: neither the authors nor a literature search could locate that reference. The only sound replacement is on-platform human data collected under this port's own parameters, which is the v2 plan. Selecting a different published RDK study would not fix this, for the reason Pilly & Seitz give.
